title: The Epidemiology of Injuries Across the Weight-Training Sports
population: Competitive athletes in weightlifting, powerlifting, bodybuilding, strongman, Highland Games and CrossFit; 20 eligible injury-epidemiology studies; not recreational runners
findings: Twenty studies were eligible; only five had a risk-of-bias score of 75% or more (low risk of bias), 14 had more than 100 participants and only four were prospective.

Bodybuilding had the lowest injury rates (0.12-0.7 injuries per lifter per year; 0.24-1 injury per 1000 hours); strongman (4.5-6.1 per 1000 hours) and Highland Games (7.5 per 1000 hours) had the highest.

The shoulder, lower back, knee, elbow and wrist or hand were generally the most common injury locations; strains, tendinitis and sprains were the most common types. Very few differences by age, sex, competitive standard or bodyweight class were found.

The authors conclude that the weight-training sports appear to have relatively low injury rates compared with common team sports, and that research is needed with prospective designs and measured exposure.
limitations: Competitive athletes of sports that use heavy loads in competition, mostly retrospective studies; no recreational lifters and no runners; rates per 1000 hours differ widely between sports. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: Second source, with the Aasa 2016 review, only for the statement that injury rates across the weight-training sports are low next to common team sports. The figures for weightlifting and powerlifting and the comparison with other non-contact sports are Aasa 2016's, not this abstract's. Both cover competitive lifters, not a recreational runner starting barbell work, so there is still no safety data for that group (the gap behind the barbell rule).
Lower back, knee and shoulder are the common sites in lifters; the engine's lower-body catalogue has no upper-body or overhead lift.
